paragraphs: Morning mist still lay over Chang’an. Beyond the eastern gate, carts laden with charcoal and vegetables had formed a queue. The drum announcing the change of watch had barely sounded when the gate guards saw a rider coming from the direction of the Luo River. Foam clotted his horse’s mane. Mud stained half his vermilion robe, but he held a gleaming black lacquer box close against his chest.
“An urgent edict from the Heavenly King, at the Luoyang palace!”

Han Ji, the aging commandant, glanced at the purple cord around the box. He had seen boxes like it before, and the clay seal looked right. When the rider offered his fish-shaped credential, Han Ji did not take it at once. “At which post station did you change horses yesterday?”
“Huayin.”
“Who is the postmaster at Huayin?”
“I bear an urgent edict, not answers to your examination.”

The man’s eyes were dark with exhaustion; he looked every bit a messenger who had ridden for two days and nights. Behind Han Ji a young soldier muttered that if the Heavenly King had died, a moment’s delay might cost them their heads. Han Ji took the credential and held it to the morning light. An old chip marred the fish’s tail, exactly as the register recorded.
“Open the east gate. The box goes first to the Secretariat, with its bearer in attendance. No detours.”
“The edict expressly orders it delivered straight to the palace.”
“Then let the Palace Guard Office send someone to collect it from the Secretariat.”

The rider tried to urge his horse through, but Han Ji laid his long halberd across the wheel-ruts. The vegetable sellers crowded behind them withdrew as one. The rider stared at the commandant, then at last handed his reins to a guard. Only then did several women carrying vegetables dare pass along the wall. They knew nothing of what might happen at court. They remembered only that the man in red had been breathing harder than his horse.

An hour later the lacquer box stood in the Hall of Supreme Polarity. Fu Hong had not slept an unbroken night in three days. Shadows lay beneath his eyes, though not a fold of his robes or cap was out of place. The imperial throne stood empty. He received the ministers from his seat below the dais, refusing the clansmen who urged him to ascend it.
“Bring in the messenger.”

The man in red gave his name as Zhao Qian, a court attendant from the Luoyang palace. Asked about the Heavenly King’s health, he said that the king had briefly awakened the previous night, sat up, and dictated a lengthy edict. When the chief minister asked whether there was a copy countersigned by Fu Rong for the officials remaining at Luoyang, Zhao replied that the bedside attendants had received a secret command and were forbidden to trouble the Duke of Yangping.
“For whom, then, was this edict written?” Fu Hong asked.

“For Your Highness, and still more for Great Qin.” Zhao Qian prostrated himself, keeping his voice low. “The Heavenly King knows that traitors have usurped authority. He ordered me to ride day and night to save the ancestral temples.”

At the word “traitors,” several men looked toward the place where Murong Chui usually stood. It was empty today. The Grand Commandant had been kept at his office to verify land deeds from Hebei and was absent from the morning audience.

They broke the seal. Beneath blackened sealing clay lay white hemp paper, covered in heavy dark strokes; at the foot shone an almost painfully vivid red impression of the Heavenly King’s seal. The chief minister began reading evenly. When he reached the revocation of the crown prince’s regency, his voice faltered.

Fu Hong was ordered back to the Eastern Palace to await further instructions. Fu Pi, commanding at Xiangyang, was to bring ten thousand picked troops into the passes and assume control of all military affairs, within and without. Grand Commandant Murong Chui was to be seized at once. Land surveys and the Qin household registers were suspended, with the former registers and holdings provisionally restored. The capital’s troops would pass under the clan military command. One final clause ordered the palace guards to seal off the Eastern Palace that very day; disobedience would be punished as defiance of an imperial edict.

For a long time no one in the hall moved. Beyond the curtain came only the rasp of a bamboo broom across the courtyard. Fu Hong took the two sheets and read them slowly. He remembered the blood his father had coughed before a Luoyang granary last year, and the orders he himself had sent to Xiangyang, allowing his elder brother to bring only a hundred men to the capital. Under this edict, his brother would arrive with ten thousand, not a hundred. And on the day Murong Chui was arrested, rumors of the old Yan kingdom would rise again across Hebei.

Fu Chengye of the imperial clan stepped forward, declaring that the king’s own edict admitted no delay by his subjects. When the general charged with the central army’s seal asked about the threefold authorization required to move troops, Fu Chengye laughed coldly. “The Heavenly King made those rules. Must he now beg his ministers for their seals?”

Fu Hong did not take the bait. His father certainly had the authority to amend an edict. But if a handwritten order arrived suddenly while he was too ill to attend court, and no one verified it, then anyone possessing a seal could speak in the name of a man on his sickbed.
He turned to Zhao Qian. “Who wrote the edict?”
“Sun Yan, Director of the Inner Attendants.”
“Where is Sun Yan now?”
“With the royal party.”
“He retired to his home three years ago. He lives south of Chang’an. I sent him medicine only last month.”
Zhao Qian swallowed. “I rode in such haste, Your Highness, that I may have confused the name.”
“And do you remember it now?”

Zhao said nothing. Fu Hong did not press him. Instead he ordered the clerks responsible for the seals to bring samples from recent years. Six sheets lay spread across the table. The old seal bore wear at one corner; the new one also had a fine diagonal crack on its right side. The impression on this supposed edict showed the old wear but none of the newer damage.

The clerk examined it several times beside the lamp, sweat gathering on his forehead. “Your Highness, the paper may simply have been too stiff for the crack to take the pigment. I dare not call it a forgery on that ground alone.”
“Well said.” Fu Hong passed the end of the edict to the ministers. “Not on one ground alone.”

The chief minister pointed out that the edict still referred to a “Palace Guard Commandant,” an office absorbed into the Palace Guard Office years earlier. Zhao Qian’s account of the duty roster at Chengming Gate also contradicted recent reports from Luoyang. Fu Chengye insisted that a sick man might readily recall an obsolete title. Argument broke out on both sides, and neither was wholly without reason.
At last Fu Hong tapped the corner of the table. It was no thunderous blow, yet the ministers gradually fell silent.
“If the edict is genuine and I refuse it today, I shall accept my punishment when my father awakens. If it is false and I obey it today, people will die. And perhaps not just one.”

He asked the Secretariat and the central army command to set down their findings separately. The Secretariat, citing the titles, the messenger’s statements, and the disputed seal, recommended sealing the order pending verification. The army command explicitly refused to summon troops from Xiangyang. Fu Hong signed the third column and bound the three opinions together in full view of the court.

“Send three mounted messengers to Luoyang. One by the official post road, one by the merchants' road, and one bearing a sample of the edict directly to the Duke of Yangping. Give each a different sealed identifier. They must not meet along the way. Until Luoyang replies, this edict shall not be carried out.”
“You dare suppress the Heavenly King’s sacred command!” Fu Chengye shouted.

“It is being held here.” Fu Hong pointed to the lacquer box. “The witnesses and the material evidence are here as well. If any gentleman objects, let him write his objection behind today’s record and sign his name.”
That quieted many of them. They were willing enough to hail the Heavenly King in court; fewer were willing to put their names beneath an unverified order to move an army.

By afternoon rumors had spread through Chang’an’s markets. Some said the Heavenly King was dead and the crown prince was concealing his death; others claimed that the edict restored estate lands and the Secretariat had dared disobey. Landowners who had lost estates sent servants everywhere for news. Soldiers newly granted deeds crowded the county offices, afraid that the plots allotted to them yesterday would be confiscated tomorrow.

Fu Hong ordered the capital prefecture to post a notice specifying what edict had been received that day, why it was being held, and how messengers had been dispatched to verify it in Luoyang. People packed the space before the placard. The first to speak was an old woman with a child in her arms. “Can we still sow our seven mu of land?”
The clerk reading the notice saw the cracks covering her hands. “The deed you held yesterday is valid today.”
“And tomorrow?”
He would not promise her a lifetime without authority. He pointed to the Secretariat’s seal on the notice. “If the order changes tomorrow, another notice will be posted here.”

The woman stared at the seal for a long while before leading the child away. She could scarcely read, but she understood that this time no one had shouted from an office doorway and taken away the field she had worked all spring.

At dusk Fu Hong went to see Murong Chui. Two extra squads of palace troops stood before the Grand Commandant’s residence; across the street, several travelers in broad hats had lingered too long. Murong Chui did not ask whether the guards had been stationed there because he was distrusted. He took the forged edict and studied it by candlelight.

“To arrest you they must borrow my father’s name; to seize the land they must destroy the Qin registers; to summon Fu Pi they must first depose the crown prince,” Fu Hong said. “How can one edict serve so many interests?”

Murong Chui ran a finger along the edge of the impression and answered slowly. “Because each of them wanted these things already. Whoever wrote the edict merely put all their wishes on one sheet of paper.”
“Do you know who wrote it?”
“Knowing who profits and knowing whose hand held the brush are two different things.”

After a pause Murong Chui suggested letting it be known that the edict would be proclaimed the next day, tempting the real conspirators to move on the granaries and offices. At first Fu Hong refused. With the Heavenly King’s fate still uncertain, a feigned maneuver might become a genuine uprising. Murong Chui did not urge recklessness; he only asked, “If no one comes tonight, what will they be waiting for tomorrow night?”
After a long silence Fu Hong said, “For us to grow tired.”

So only a handful were told. In public the Secretariat took down its notice, saying the sample had been sent back for verification and a new proclamation would follow tomorrow. In secret, documents bearing the three seals quietly repositioned the palace guards. The arsenal and gates kept their regular watches, with no rash changes of personnel. Only a few guards remained at Murong Chui’s residence, lest the clatter of armor throughout the streets alarm the people.

Rain began in the hour of hai. Murong Chui sat in the main hall beneath a lamp. Two unsent family letters lay before him, one to an old friend in Ye, the other to his household in Guanzhong. He had signed both with only his name, neither “Prince of Wu” nor “Grand Commandant.”

Someone knocked at the gate ring, claiming that the Court of Judicial Review had come under the Heavenly King’s edict to arrest a treasonous minister. The guards demanded the document bearing three seals; the men outside said the endorsements would be supplied tomorrow. Murong Chui himself stepped beneath the eaves and asked who led them. The man removed his broad hat. It was Fu Chengye.
“A few words in court, and tonight you come with soldiers?”
Fu Chengye held up a copy of the handwritten edict, his jaw clenched. “If you are innocent, why be afraid to come with me?”
“I am afraid. And I fear the men who follow you through this gate will never come out again.”

The front gate opened a crack. As a dozen false judicial guards crossed the threshold, lanterns hidden beneath cloaks flared along the outer street. Palace troops swept in from the ward entrance on both flanks. Fu Chengye drew his sword, but before he could swing it, halberds had pinned his household soldiers against the wall. Several men were wounded inside the residence; Murong Chui ordered that no captive was to be killed without cause.

Farther away the alarm bell sounded at the arsenal. Another group had arrived with tokens from the old military command, hoping to seize the weapons. The gate guards let them into the outer yard and locked the outer doors only when they began distributing armor. At the Secretariat archives, window bars were torn loose and twelve night intruders made for the household registers and land surveys, some carrying slow-burning fuses, others burlap sacks. A junior clerk took a knife wound rather than surrender his records, pushing a wooden compartment of boundary-survey appeals into a hidden recess behind the wall. When palace troops arrived, inkstones were overturned and bloody handprints covered the papers.

At the western gate they also intercepted a horse trader preparing to leave the city. Several secret letters lay beneath his saddle: one to Xiangyang claiming the crown prince had been deposed; one to Hebei announcing Murong Chui’s death that night; and one to Guanzhong landowners promising that the new registers had all been burned. The letters told different stories, yet the same misspelling appeared at the foot of each, as though one hurried scribe had donned three disguises.

At dawn an urgent dispatch entered Chang’an from the Luoyang palace. This time Fu Rong’s private letter matched the copy retained at court. Fu Jian had awakened at intervals but still could not speak. The royal seal remained locked away and unopened; he had issued no command to depose the prince, summon Fu Pi, or arrest Murong Chui. The false seal had been copied from an old impression, omitting the crack that had appeared later. There was proof at last.

Fu Hong did not rush to label the more than three hundred prisoners a single conspiracy. He ordered the judicial officers to separate their cases: those who cut the false seal, those who carried the edict, those who tried to mobilize troops, those who stole land deeds amid the confusion. Each would answer for his own actions. Merely urging obedience to the edict in court would not be treated as a crime. Some complained that Fu Chengye had not been struck down at once. Fu Hong replied only that two guards had already died before Murong Chui’s gate; killing one more man could not mend the failures of that night.

When the sun was high, the government granary south of the city opened as usual. The old woman from the previous day received her ration of rice, though the hand resting on the wooden measure still trembled. She heard the crowd say the forged edict had been exposed. She did not ask who had plotted it. She clutched the grain against her chest and hurried home to light her stove.

Just then a military clerk burst into the Secretariat, his face ashen. He carried the night watch log from a residence in the western city. Between the hours of hai and chou, a forged redeployment order had drawn the guards away. Yao Chang and his two elderly servants had vanished. The mud in a disused drainage ditch beyond the side wall had been freshly disturbed.

Fu Hong closed the dossier. The Heavenly King in Luoyang had yet to wake fully; the counterfeit royal seal in Chang’an had been found. But a man confined for years, with old connections both at court and among the Qiang, had at last vanished in the same night.

Morning sunlight lit the steps outside the hall; rainwater still stood on the white marble. Fu Hong ordered the latest dispatch posted in every ward and told the northwest checkpoints to examine people, vehicles, and travel passes. He did not allow the clerk to write, “Yao Chang was the mastermind behind the forged edict.”
“Write that he escaped confinement,” he said. “For the rest, record each charge only when we have proved it.”

He returned from below the empty throne to his desk. Someone asked whether today’s business should await a fresh edict from the Heavenly King. Fu Hong shook his head and opened the household register whose corner had been stained with blood the night before.
“First let us finish today’s work.”
